runs.title: Stone Circle zone — standing stones, pool, autumn tree, drifting lights
runs.journal:
I built the **Stone Circle**, the world's first place, 22 m north of spawn. You walk a short path of stepping stones and pass through a gate. Inside are seven standing stones around a still pool, with an autumn tree growing on an island in the middle and a few warm lights drifting slowly between the stones. Everything is procedural: canvas textures for the lichened stone and the curved flagstones, a recursive tree, and instanced grass and leaves. I picked something calm and central because an empty world needs a landmark to come back to. The circle can be the hub that later places branch out from.
Next: maybe paths leaving the circle toward a second place, or making the pool respond to the player's hands in VR. The grass is still simple cones and could look better.

runs.title: Meadowlands zone (meadow floor, hills, groves, brook, footbridge, trail, brook sound); slimmer circle tufts
runs.journal:
I built the **Meadowlands**, the land itself. On day 1 the Stone Circle sat on an endless grey plane, and it looked like a model on a table. Now a coloured meadow floor covers everything. Low hills rise beyond about 85 m (the flat middle is there because walking doesn't follow terrain) and fade into the haze. Groves of autumn trees and dark conifers are scattered on the hills, and there are drifts of wildflowers and grass. A brook winds down a valley past the west side of the circle. A packed-earth trail leaves the circle westward, crosses the brook on an arched plank footbridge between two lantern posts, and ends in a grove of yellow birches. The brook is the first sound in the world: synthesized burbling that gets louder as you approach the water. I also slimmed the circle's cone-shaped grass tufts so they match the new grass.
Next: the birch grove at (−70, −32) is waiting to become a place, perhaps somewhere to sit or something hidden among the trunks. An east trail could follow. The water is a bit dark and flat, and the flowers are only flat petals; both could be richer.

runs.title: Birch Glade (pavilion, tuned wind chimes, wind, falling leaves); clear grove centre; WORLD.md and journal
runs.journal:
I built the **Birch Glade** at the end of the west trail. I cleared the middle of the birch grove and covered it in fallen yellow leaves. In the clearing stands a small open hexagonal pavilion of dark timber, with a bench facing back down the trail toward the stone circle and an unlit lantern hanging from the roof. Six clusters of brass wind chimes hang from the eaves. Everything in the glade answers to one slow, gusting wind: the chimes swing and ring on their own when it picks up, leaves shake loose from the birches and drift down, and a soft hiss in the branches swells and fades. The chimes are tuned to a pentatonic scale, so whatever the wind plays sounds right. You can ring them yourself by brushing them with a hand in VR, or by looking at one and clicking on desktop. The sound is positional, so each cluster rings from its own corner. I wanted the first place you walk *to* to be somewhere to stop and listen, which also extends the world's sound beyond the brook.
Next: the east is still empty. The brook valley running north into the hills invites a walk upstream to its source. Birdsong would also help the meadow feel alive.

runs.title: Reed Pond (east trail, jetty, rowboat, reeds, lily pads, willow, heron, dragonflies, frogs, birdsong, stone skipping with ripple shader)
runs.journal:
I built **Reed Pond**, east of the Stone Circle, so the hub now has a place on each side: the glade to the west, the pond to the east. A new trail leads straight out of the circle to a plank jetty over the water. Reeds and cattails grow in beds around the shore and sway in the wind. Lily pads float on the water with a few water lilies among them, and a rowboat with its oars shipped is tied to the end of the jetty. A big weeping willow trails its strands down to the north bank. A grey heron stands in the eastern shallows and now and then stabs at a fish, dragonflies dart and dip, frogs croak from the reeds, and a bird sings in the willow (the first birdsong in the world). The water is a custom shader that tints with depth, reflects the sky, catches the sun and spreads rings whenever something touches it: a rising fish, a dipping dragonfly, the heron's beak. The game in it is skipping stones. Stand on the jetty and click, or pull a trigger in VR, and a flat stone skims across the pond, plinking and leaving a trail of rings before it sinks. I wanted a place you could *do* something small and satisfying, not only look and listen. One bug I caught: the ripple rings didn't show at first, because Three's `UniformsUtils.merge` clones the uniform array.
Next: the brook valley north toward its source is the obvious next walk. The circle's own pool could borrow the ripple shader so it answers to hands in VR. The willow still looks a little like a curtain when seen against the sun.

runs.title: The Old Mill (watermill on the brook, south trail, gearing, millstones, sluice gate, sounds)
runs.journal:
I built **the Old Mill**, the first place south of the hub. A new trail leaves from just behind spawn and runs south-west across the meadow to a watermill on the brook's east bank, about 60 m from the stone circle. The house has a stone ground floor, a half-timbered upper storey with warm-lit windows, and a steep shingled roof. A big undershot wheel turns in the brook beside it, throwing spray from its paddles over a patch of foam, and a low weir of stones upstream adds its own white water. You can walk in through the open door. Inside, the axle comes through the wall and turns a pegged pit wheel, which drives a wallower and a great spur wheel, and those turn the runner millstone on its platform under the hopper. Flour dust drifts in the lantern light, and sacks lean against the whitewashed walls. Every gear turns at its own ratio, all driven by the wheel. You can hear it: water churning, each paddle slapping in, the axle groaning in its bearing, and inside, the low pulsing rumble of the stones. The thing to *do* is the sluice gate: turn its handwheel (click it, or trigger it in VR) and the board drops, the water leaves the wheel, and the whole mill coasts slowly to silence. Open it again and everything spins back up. I picked a mill because the brook had been running past the world for three days without doing anything, and because a place whose parts all move together is satisfying to stand inside. One bug took a while to find: the ceiling was invisible because a solid beam slab I'd meant as a trim band covered the whole footprint just below it.
Next: the south-east meadow is still empty. The brook's source to the north can't really be walked to, because walking doesn't follow hills, so it may have to be a place seen from afar. The mill could have a millpond or a miller's cottage. Larks over the open meadow would still help.

runs.title: The Orchard (walled apple orchard in the SE meadow, hives and bees, pickable/throwable apples, robin song)
runs.journal:
I built **the Orchard** in the empty south-east meadow, so the two trails from spawn now fork: south-west to the mill, south-east to the orchard. Through a gap in a lichened dry-stone wall, past a five-bar gate standing open, eleven old apple trees grow in loose rows, with gnarled trunks and crowns turning from green to autumn yellow. Each tree carries its own variety: deep red, orange-streaked, green-gold, russet. Windfalls lie in the grass, a ladder leans against one tree with baskets of picked apples at its foot, and a bench sits in the gap where a tree is missing. Three white beehives stand along the east wall, and bees work between them, the trees, and a bed of purple Michaelmas daisies along the south wall. You can hear the hives humming, and a robin sings from a different treetop every so often. The thing to *do* is pick apples. Click one on a branch and it snaps off and drops with a thud, then rolls. Click a fallen one and you toss it. Click a crown and the tree shakes loose a few more. In VR you can grab any apple off a tree or the ground and throw it, and the wall stops it. After the mill, a place full of machinery, I wanted somewhere slower and more hand-sized, and apples are the most natural thing in the world to reach for.
Next: the brook's source to the north is still unvisited. The orchard could get a cider press. The world's sounds are now spread over five separate AudioContexts, so one shared context would be worth considering. Larks over the open meadow would still help.

runs.title: North Pasture (sheep flock, dry-stone fold with hurdle gate, shepherd's hut, whistle-to-follow herding, bleats, bell, skylark)
runs.journal:
I built **the North Pasture**, so every direction from the stone circle now leads somewhere. A new trail leaves the north edge of the circle and runs up the open meadow to a shepherd's hut on iron wheels. It is painted green, with an arched tin roof, a warm window, a crook leaning by the steps, and smoke drifting from the stove pipe. On the pasture between the hut and the trees grazes a small flock of fourteen sheep: eleven ewes (one black), and three lambs. They wander and graze with their heads down, lift their heads to watch you when you come close, and shy away if you walk at them, and the alarm spreads through the flock. One of them wears a bell. Off to the side stands a round dry-stone fold with a hay rack and a water trough inside, a wooden hurdle gate, and an unlit lantern on the gatepost. The thing to *do* is to bring the flock in. Whistle (click on the open pasture, or pull a trigger in VR) and for a while they follow you. Walk into the fold and they come round to the gap and crowd in around the hay. Step out, swing the gate shut, and when every sheep is inside the lantern lights, they bleat contentedly, and most of them lie down. Above it all a skylark sings, the meadow birdsong I'd been meaning to add since day 3. The bleats are synthesized: a buzzing tone through vowel-shaped filters with a quaver in it, higher for the lambs. To check the herding I ran the zone's update loop headlessly with a scripted walk, since the snapshot can't click. All fourteen followed me in and stayed, and the gate lit the lantern.
Next: with all five directions filled, the world could deepen rather than spread, for example a cider press in the orchard, a millpond, or touch ripples in the circle's pool. A place seen from afar on the hills would also give the horizon something to look at. Six zones now each run their own AudioContext, and that is worth consolidating at some point.

runs.title: penguin avatar — third-person camera, collisions, ground following, swimming, belly-sliding
runs.journal:
The owner asked for an avatar, a penguin if possible, with a third-person view and no glitching through floors or walls. I liked the idea, so the world now has its first inhabitant who is *you*. **The Penguin** is a small round emperor-ish penguin: a black back, a white belly, gold ear patches, bright eyes, an orange beak, and orange feet. It waddles when you walk, rocking from side to side with its flippers held out, and turns to face where it's going. When you stop it glances around. Space makes it hop with a flap. Sprinting makes it drop onto its belly and toboggan across the meadow, which is what penguins actually do when they're in a hurry. Walk into the Reed Pond or the stone circle's pool and it swims, low in the water, leaving ripples on the pond.
The camera sits behind and above it and shortens when a wall or the ground gets in the way. Inside the mill it stays under the ceiling. The trick that made this possible without touching the engine: the camera only moves back while the frame is being drawn, then returns to the penguin's eye. So every place built so far (the chimes, the apples, the sluice gate, the whistle for the sheep) still works from where the penguin stands, and the crosshair still aims down the same line. V switches back to first person.
The world was also solid for the first time. Walls, standing stones, tree trunks (all four hundred of them), the mill, the hut, the hives, and the fold all stop you now. The fold's gate gap blocks only while the hurdle is shut. The ground pushes back too: you step up onto the stone circle's mound, the pavilion deck, the jetty, and over the arch of the footbridge. And because walking now follows the land, **the hills are climbable**, which they never were before. In VR you stay in first person, but look down and there's a penguin body beneath you, and the same walls stop you.
I tested it headlessly by walking the player at things: into the orchard wall (it stops at the wall face), through the gate, into the mill wall and through its door, across the bridge, into the pond, and up the hills.
Next: now that the hills can be walked, a place up on them (a lookout, a cairn, the brook's source) finally makes sense. The sheep could notice the penguin, and the penguin could have a few sounds of its own: footsteps, a splash, a squawk.

runs.title: the shepherd's hut can be entered — interior with stove, kettle, bunk, sleeping collie; penguin collisions/ground/camera for the hut
runs.journal:
The owner noticed that the shepherd's hut (the "wagon") couldn't be entered. Since day 8 it had been a solid box for collisions, and the door was only painted on. That was a good nudge, because the hut's warm window had been promising an inside for two days. Now **you can go in**. Climb the three steps and walk through the open door into a small, lamplit room under the curved roof, lined with cream boards. A bunk with a patchwork quilt fills the far end, and an oil lamp burns on a table under the window next to a mug and a book. A row of jars sits on the shelf, and a coat hangs by the door. At the near end a little cast-iron stove glows on its hearth and crackles, and its pipe goes up to the chimney you've seen smoking from the pasture. The shepherd's collie is asleep on the rag rug. Come close and it lifts its head and follows you with its eyes. Give it a click and it thumps its tail.
The thing to *do* is to make tea, or at least boil the kettle. Click the kettle and it moves from the hearth to the hob. After a while steam starts to curl from the spout, then the lid rattles and it whistles until you take it off. The window is real glass now, so from inside you can watch the sheep, and from outside you can see the lamp and the stove's glow.
On the penguin's side, the hut became four walls with a gap for the door, plus the bunk, table, stove, and dog as obstacles. The floor and steps are walkable. Inside, the camera stays under the roof. The sheep still treat the hut as solid, which seems right. I tested it by walking the player in headlessly: up the steps, through the door, into the bunk, the back wall, and the end wall, then out again.
Next: maybe a place up on the hills, now that they're walkable. The collie could also come out and help herd the sheep one day.

runs.title: Beacon Hill — hill path, summit with toposcope, cairn, bench, and a beacon the far hills answer; groundMeshHeight for the penguin
runs.journal:
I built **Beacon Hill**, the first place up on the hills, now that the penguin can climb them. A worn path branches off the Reed Pond trail, passes the willow, runs through a grove, and climbs north-east past little waymark posts to a bare summit about 32 m above the meadow. From the top you can see the whole land laid out: the stone circle, the pond, the mill and the brook, the glade, and the sheep by the hut. Up there is a stone bench facing back the way you came, and a **toposcope**: a bronze table on a stone pillar, engraved with a compass rose and an arrow to every place in the world, each with its name and distance. Beside it is a **cairn**. Click it and you add a stone, which drops onto the pile with a clack, and the cairn remembers how many you've added across visits.
The thing to *do* is the **beacon**, an iron fire basket on a tall pole. Light it and it whooshes up into flame and sparks, and a column of smoke leans away on the wind, tall enough to see from the stone circle. A few seconds later a faint horn sounds from far away, and a second beacon flares on Gorse Top to the north. Then Long Ridge, far to the west, answers, and finally Hob's Knoll in the south-east, until fires are burning on hills all round the horizon. They burn for a few minutes and die down, and you can light them again.
Underneath, I found that far from the middle the drawn ground is made of big flat triangles that don't match the smooth terrain function, so things (and the penguin) floated or sank by tens of centimetres on the hills. The meadowlands now exports `groundMeshHeight`, the height of the ground as actually drawn (checked against raycasts: exact), and the penguin walks on it. I couldn't click in the headless snapshots, so I checked the lit beacons by lighting them at start-up for a test render, then removed that.
Next: the three answering hills only hold a fire basket each and could become places of their own. The brook's source in the north-west hills is still unvisited. The collie could still come out and help with the sheep.

runs.title: no whistling from inside the shepherd's hut
runs.journal:
First, a small fix the owner pointed out: from inside the shepherd's hut you could still whistle, and the whole flock would come charging at the hut. Now a click indoors doesn't reach the sheep. They can't hear you in there, and the collie is asleep anyway.
The main work was **Brook Head**, the source of the brook. Day 10's journal mentioned it as unvisited, and when I went to look I found something odd: about 120 m up the valley the brook simply vanished. The water ribbon lay on the smooth terrain function, and the coarse far ground mesh covered it (the same problem Beacon Hill ran into). The water is now draped on the ground as drawn, so you can see the brook winding all the way up its valley into the north-west hills. A new path runs up the east bank from the footbridge to where it begins.
At the top there's a stone spring basin, banked with turf, under a curved mossy wall. Water pours from a carved spout into the basin, and the basin spills over a low lip stone into the brook. A rowan with red berries leans over it, with ferns at the wall's foot and boulders scattered about. A plaque in the wall reads "Brook Head — set a leaf on the water". Next to the basin is a heap of big fallen leaves. Click the water (or the heap) and a curled leaf with a twig mast and a little sail drifts across the basin, tips over the lip, and sails off down the **whole brook**: down the valley, under the footbridge, past the mill, and on to the far south-west. You can follow it the whole way, about three minutes to the bridge. And on the footbridge itself you can drop sticks, pale and dark ones in turn, and race them under the bridge.
I couldn't click in the headless renders, so I checked the floaters by launching a few at start-up for one test render (leaves in the brook below the spring, a stick downstream of the bridge), then took that out. There's one known sliver near (−141, −246) where a crease in the coarse hill mesh pokes through the water.
Next: the upper valley is bare and could use alders or thorn trees along the water. The leaf boats could bump against the mill's wheel, or end up in a pool you could find them in. The collie still wants to come out and help with the sheep.
